newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Forum says low inflation, reform keys to growth.
newsitem.headline: Forum says low inflation, reform keys to growth.

text.p: From Argentina to Austria, the message from some of the world's top economic decision-makers gathered here is that only deep, often painful, structural reform and low inflation can guarantee prosperity.

Reforms of still too rigid labour markets and other economic practices in much of western Europe and swollen state sectors in parts of the developing world were a pre-condition for sustained growth in an increasingly competitive world.

The theme was hammered home at meetings in this Swiss mountain resort that bring together each year government leaders, top figures from business and academics from a host of countries to debate the state of the world.

"There is an overwhelming consensus, north and south, east and west, to say that the basis for sustained growth is low inflation, appropriate fiscal policies, appropriate monetary policies," said one European central banker.
"The message coming out of here is that stability and (financial market) confidence is of the essence. There is fantastic consensus on this point," he said.
"Appropriate reforms that would permit the creation of more jobs is the other part of the equation," he added.

Argentina offers a case in point. Once a world-beater in the inflation stakes, the country has now one of the best international records with prices rising less than one percent in 1996 -- a better performance than any of the world's leading industrial nations.

Despite high unemployment of some 17 percent and looming elections, Finance Minister Roque Fernandez was adamant here that there was no chance of the Peronist government of President Carlos Menem easing its tough line on prices.
"There can be no trade-off between inflation and employment," he said.

Argentine officials said that the jobless rate, uncomfortably high for a Peronist movement with historic links to organised labour, stemmed from a shake-up of the public sector and would in any case not be responsive to any quick economic fix such as boosting consumer demand.

In western Europe, where free market economics have taken firm root over the past decade, many governments have still to bite the bullet on unpopular labour reforms that could often translate into easier hiring and firing for firms.
But with European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) due to be launched in January 1999, finance ministers attending the World Economic Forum warned that such decisions could not be long delayed.
"Removing national labour market rigidities is now urgent," Spain's Finance Minister Rodrigo Rato said.
